tree.title: Biology EOC Review
tree.description: Concept review for the NC Biology End-of-Course exam, organized by standard.

children.title: Cell Structure & Transport
children.description: Organelle jobs, prokaryote vs eukaryote, plant vs animal cells, and how materials cross the membrane by diffusion, osmosis, and active transport.

children.title: Organelle Functions
children.description: Each organelle's structure fits the job it does for the cell.

teach.headline: Each Organelle Has a Job
teach.body:
A cell is a division of labor. The **nucleus** stores DNA and directs the cell. **Ribosomes** build proteins by translating mRNA into amino acids. **Mitochondria** release energy as ATP through cellular respiration. **Chloroplasts** capture sunlight for photosynthesis (in plants). The **vacuole** stores water and materials.

Structure fits function: lose an organelle and the cell loses its matching ability — no ribosomes means no new proteins.
teach.mnemonic: RIBOSOME = PROTEIN PRINTER. MITOCHONDRION = POWER PLANT. CHLOROPLAST = SOLAR PANEL.
teach.poweredIdea: An organelle's structure fits its job: ribosomes build proteins, mitochondria release energy.

data.prompt: mRNA is translated into amino acids to build proteins at the _____.

data.story: A mutation leaves a plant cell with no functioning ribosomes, though every other organelle is normal.
data.question: What can this cell no longer do?
data.answer: Translate mRNA into amino acids to make proteins
options: Translate mRNA into amino acids to make proteins
Store its DNA in the nucleus
data.explanation: Ribosomes are the site of translation. Without them the cell cannot assemble proteins, even if its DNA and other organelles are intact.

data.story: In a plant cell, the vacuole stores the water used during photosynthesis. A mutation makes the vacuole much smaller.
data.question: What is the most likely effect on photosynthesis?
data.answer: Less water can be stored, so the rate of photosynthesis decreases.
options: Less water can be stored, so the rate of photosynthesis decreases.
More water can be stored, so photosynthesis speeds up.
The cell releases more water, so photosynthesis speeds up.
Photosynthesis is unaffected because the vacuole is not involved.
data.explanation: A smaller vacuole holds less of the water photosynthesis depends on, lowering the reaction rate.

achievement.flavor: You match each organelle to its job and predict what breaks when one goes missing.

children.authorNotes: NC LS.Bio.1.3 (organelle structure/function and interactions). Maps to released items #31 (ribosome/translation) and #10 (vacuole/photosynthesis). Reworded, not reproduced. Goes deeper than biochem.cells.organelles; no biochem.* id reuse.

children.title: Prokaryote vs Eukaryote
children.description: What distinguishes simple cells without a nucleus from complex cells with membrane-bound organelles.

teach.headline: Eukaryotes Box Up Their Parts
teach.body:
**Prokaryotes** (bacteria) are small and simple. Their DNA floats free in the cytoplasm — there is no nucleus — and they have no membrane-bound organelles. But they still have **ribosomes**, a cell membrane, and (usually) a cell wall, so they make proteins and stay alive.

**Eukaryotes** (plants, animals, fungi, protists) are larger and complex: their DNA is packed inside a membrane-bound **nucleus**, and they have organelles like mitochondria.
teach.mnemonic: PRO = BEFORE the nucleus. EU = TRUE nucleus. KARYON = NUT. Bacteria carry DNA with no nucleus box.
teach.poweredIdea: Prokaryotes lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotes have both.

data.prompt: A cell with no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles is a _____ cell.

data.story: Under a microscope, a cell shows a cell wall and ribosomes but no nucleus, no mitochondria, and no chloroplasts.
data.question: Which type of cell is this most likely to be?
data.explanation: Lacking a nucleus and all membrane-bound organelles, while still having ribosomes and a wall, is the signature of a prokaryote.

data.paragraph: Because prokaryotes have no nucleus, they have no DNA at all, so they cannot make proteins or reproduce.
data.bugPhrase: they have no DNA at all, so they cannot make proteins or reproduce
data.hint: A nucleus is a container for DNA — is it the only place DNA can be?
data.canonicalFix: Prokaryotes do have DNA; it simply floats free in the cytoplasm instead of inside a nucleus. They have ribosomes, make proteins, and reproduce by binary fission.
data.poweredIdea: No nucleus does not mean no DNA — prokaryotic DNA just isn't membrane-bound.

data.mnemonic: EU = TRUE. KARYON = NUCLEUS. A EUkaryote has a TRUE, membrane-bound nucleus.

question.prompt: Which structure do eukaryotes have that prokaryotes lack?

achievement.flavor: You spot a prokaryote by its missing nucleus and organelles — without claiming it has no DNA.

children.authorNotes: NC LS.Bio.1.4 (compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells). Maps to released item #4 (identify the prokaryote from an organelle chart). Debug-the-claim targets the 'no nucleus = no DNA' trap. No biochem.* id reuse.

children.title: Plant vs Animal Cells
children.description: The three structures plant cells add to the shared eukaryotic toolkit.

teach.headline: Plant Cells Add Three Parts
teach.body:
Plant and animal cells are both **eukaryotic**, so both have a nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, and a cell membrane.

Plant cells add three structures animal cells do not have: a rigid **cell wall** for support, **chloroplasts** for photosynthesis, and a large **central vacuole** that stores water and keeps the cell firm.

![Cross-sections of plant and animal cells with labeled organelles](/content/bio-eoc/figures/bio_eoc_plant_animal_cells.svg)

figures.alt: Labeled cross-sections of plant and animal cells showing cell wall, chloroplasts, and central vacuole in the plant cell
figures.caption: Plant cells add a cell wall, chloroplasts, and a large central vacuole.

teach.mnemonic: PLANTS GET WALL + CHLOROPLAST + BIG VACUOLE. Animals travel light — no wall, no chloroplast.
teach.poweredIdea: Plant cells add a cell wall, chloroplasts, and a large central vacuole that animal cells lack.

data.prompt: The organelle that lets plant cells capture light for photosynthesis is the _____.
data.hint: Green, found only in plant cells

data.prompt: In the diagram, photosynthesis occurs in the _____.
data.hint: Green organelle in the plant cell only

data.correct: Found in plant cells but not animal cells
distractors: Found in animal cells but not plant cells

data.story: A student examines a cell with a rigid outer cell wall, several chloroplasts, and one large central vacuole.
data.question: What kind of cell is it?
data.explanation: A cell wall, chloroplasts, and a large central vacuole together point to a plant cell.

achievement.flavor: You name the wall, chloroplast, and central vacuole as the parts that mark a plant cell.

children.authorNotes: NC LS.Bio.1.3, 1.4. Reinforces the plant-cell diagram items on the released form. Original content; goes deeper than biochem.cells.compare. No biochem.* id reuse.

children.title: Passive vs Active Transport
children.description: When the membrane moves materials for free and when it has to spend ATP.

teach.headline: Going With or Against the Gradient
teach.body:
The cell membrane is **selectively permeable** — it controls what enters and exits to maintain homeostasis.

**Passive transport** (diffusion, osmosis, facilitated diffusion) moves substances from **high to low** concentration and costs no energy. **Active transport** moves substances from **low to high** — against the gradient — and requires **ATP**, usually through protein pumps.
teach.mnemonic: DOWNHILL = FREE (passive). UPHILL = PAY ATP (active). High-to-low needs no energy.
teach.poweredIdea: Passive transport flows high-to-low with no energy; active transport pumps low-to-high using ATP.

data.prompt: The movement of molecules from high to low concentration without using energy is _____.

data.correct: Moves low to high and requires ATP
distractors: Moves high to low and uses no energy
Is just another name for diffusion

data.paragraph: Diffusion uses the cell's ATP to push molecules from where they are scarce to where they are already crowded.
data.bugPhrase: uses the cell's ATP to push molecules from where they are scarce to where they are already crowded
data.hint: Which direction does diffusion go, and does it cost energy?
data.canonicalFix: Diffusion is passive: it uses no ATP and moves molecules from crowded (high concentration) toward scarce (low concentration). Active transport is the one that spends ATP to go the other way.
data.poweredIdea: Diffusion is free and goes high-to-low; spending ATP to go low-to-high is active transport.

data.story: Oxygen is concentrated in the blood and scarce inside a nearby body cell. Oxygen drifts from the blood into the cell, and the cell spends no energy doing it.
data.question: What type of transport is this?
data.explanation: Movement from high to low concentration with no energy cost is passive transport — here, diffusion.

achievement.flavor: You decide whether the membrane moves a molecule for free or has to burn ATP to push it uphill.

children.authorNotes: NC LS.Bio.1.3 (membrane structure/function in transport). Debug-the-claim targets the 'diffusion needs energy / goes low-to-high' trap. Deeper than biochem.transport.types. No biochem.* id reuse.

children.title: Osmosis & Tonicity
children.description: Which way water crosses a membrane and what it does to plant and animal cells.

teach.headline: Water Chases Solute Across Membranes
teach.body:
**Osmosis** is the diffusion of water across a membrane. Water moves toward the side with **more solute** (and therefore less water).

In a **hypertonic** surrounding (more solute outside), water leaves the cell — animal cells shrivel and plant cells lose turgor and wilt. In a **hypotonic** surrounding (less solute outside), water enters — animal cells may burst, while plant cells gain firm **turgor pressure**. **Isotonic** means no net movement.
teach.mnemonic: HYPER = MORE SALT OUTSIDE → water OUT, cell shrinks. HYPO = less salt out → water IN, cell swells.
teach.poweredIdea: In osmosis, water moves across a membrane toward the higher solute concentration.

data.story: A gardener accidentally waters a wilting houseplant with very salty water, and the plant wilts even more.
data.question: Why did the salty water make the wilting worse?
data.answer: The salty water is hypertonic, so water moved out of the cells and they lost turgor pressure.
options: The salty water is hypertonic, so water moved out of the cells and they lost turgor pressure.
The salty water is hypotonic, so water rushed into the cells and burst them.
The salt entered the cells and replaced the water, firming them up.
Salt blocks photosynthesis, which is the only cause of wilting.
data.explanation: More solute outside than inside pulls water out of the cells. Plant cells lose turgor pressure and droop.

data.scenario: A plant cell is placed in a strong salt solution and watched under a microscope.
data.predictPrompt: What will happen to the plant cell?
predictOptions: Water rushes into the cell and it swells
Water leaves the cell; it loses turgor and the membrane pulls away from the wall
Salt moves into the cell until inside and outside match
Nothing happens because the cell wall blocks all movement
data.runNarrative: The salt solution is hypertonic. Water diffuses out of the cell toward the higher solute outside. The cell loses turgor pressure and its membrane pulls inward away from the wall — plasmolysis.
data.truthSummary: In osmosis it is water that crosses the membrane, moving toward the saltier side. The solute itself is not what moves here.

bugCandidates.label: I said the salt moved into the cell to balance the concentrations
bugCandidates.explanation: Osmosis moves water, not salt. Water exits toward the saltier outside; the salt does not flood in.

bugCandidates.label: I forgot that water moves toward the higher solute concentration
bugCandidates.explanation: Important rule, but the headline error here is treating the salt as the thing that moves.

bugCandidates.label: I assumed the cell wall stops all water movement
bugCandidates.explanation: The wall is rigid but porous to water; the membrane controls movement, not the wall.

data.poweredIdea: In a hypertonic solution, water leaves the cell — the water moves, not the salt.

data.prompt: A solution with a higher solute concentration than the cell is described as _____.

data.term: Hypotonic solution (less solute outside the cell)
distractors: Water moves out of the cell
There is no net movement of water

achievement.flavor: You predict which way water crosses a membrane and why a salted plant cell wilts.
